patterns.check: Look for duties or meanings left to guidance, letters or FAQs. Ask whether regulated parties treat these as binding in practice, whether notice and comment applies, and where the public can find them.

patterns.name: Private and industry standards
patterns.plain: Requiring compliance with industry or private standards lets standards bodies decide what the rule requires, and regulated parties are heavily represented in those bodies.
patterns.fix: Specify required outcomes in the bill, adopt standards through agency rulemaking and require balanced participation in standards bodies.
patterns.check: Find duties tied to industry, consensus or private standards. Ask who writes them, who takes part, whether the public can read them, and whether the legislature or agency adopts them.
patterns.ex_ai: AI bills can require compliance with industry or consensus AI standards, which lets the bodies that write those standards decide what the rule requires, and developers are heavily represented in those bodies.

patterns.name: Delegation through several layers
patterns.plain: When authority passes from an agency to a sub-agency and then to regional or local bodies, each level adds to the discretion until the original mandate is hard to recognize.
patterns.fix: Limit how many levels a delegation may pass through, and require reporting on how each level applies the mandate.
patterns.check: Trace each delegation from the statute to the body that finally applies it. Ask how many levels there are, what limits each level, and who reports on how the mandate is applied.

patterns.name: Certification gatekeepers
patterns.plain: Compliance through certified processes or accredited bodies can be delayed if the certifying capacity does not exist, and can depend on certifiers who are paid by the parties they certify.
patterns.fix: Build certification capacity before the duty applies, limit conflicts of interest among certifiers and allow alternatives.
patterns.check: Find every duty met through certified products, accredited bodies or approved methods. Ask whether those certifiers exist at enactment, who pays them, and what a covered party does if none is available.
patterns.ex_ai: AI bills can tie compliance to certified audits or accredited evaluators that may not exist yet, or that are paid by the developers they assess.

patterns.name: Incorporation as amended
patterns.plain: When a bill references standards as amended from time to time, the law's content changes without a new vote, and whoever maintains the document controls that content.
cues: as amended from time to time
patterns.fix: Fix the referenced version to a specific date and require review before changes are adopted.
patterns.check: Find each reference to a standard or document 'as amended'. Ask who can change that document, whether the legislature reviews changes, and whether the version is fixed by date.

patterns.name: Stacked advisory bodies
patterns.plain: Seats set aside for industry or members chosen for industry experience can give regulated parties a leading role in drafting the rules.
patterns.fix: Set balanced membership with public interest seats, conflict of interest rules and published recommendations.
patterns.check: Read who sits on each advisory body and who picks them. Ask whether seats are reserved for the parties being regulated, whether public interest seats exist, and whether recommendations must be published or can bind the agency.
patterns.ex_ai: AI bills can reserve advisory seats for developers or members chosen for technical expertise, which can give them the leading role in drafting the rules.

patterns.name: Record and comment flooding
patterns.plain: Record requirements and duties to respond to comments favor those who submit large volumes of material, which can be used to build a litigation record or to overwhelm review.
patterns.fix: Allow the agency to group duplicate comments and limit response duty to distinct issues.
patterns.check: Read the record and comment duties placed on decision makers. Ask whether duplicate or bulk submissions must each be answered, and whether the agency may group them.
patterns.ex_ai: AI bills can favor large volumes of submissions that build a litigation record or overwhelm agency review.

patterns.name: Stakeholder process design
patterns.plain: Consensus requirements in stakeholder processes can let the best organized participants block a decision, and weighting by expertise or short timelines can push other participants aside.
patterns.fix: Set balanced membership, decisions by majority vote or with stated reasons, adequate time, and agency authority to make the final decision.
patterns.check: Find any advisory or standard-setting group. Ask who sits on it, how it decides, whether a consensus requirement lets one participant block a result, how long it has, and whether the agency may decide differently from the group's recommendation.
patterns.ex_ai: Consensus requirements in stakeholder processes let industry block decisions, and weighting by expertise or short timelines can leave civil society groups out.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on telecom standards could require consensus of a working group, so any single large member can block a rule.

patterns.name: Comment period timing
patterns.plain: Short comment windows for complex rules, especially across holidays, limit how much the public and experts can take part.
patterns.fix: Set comment periods in proportion to complexity and allow extension on request.
patterns.check: Find comment, notice or hearing periods. Ask how long they run relative to the complexity of the proposal, whether they span holidays, and whether extensions are available.
patterns.ex_ai: Short comment windows for complex rules, including over holidays, limit public participation.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A land use rule of several hundred pages might open for comment for thirty days over a holiday period.

patterns.name: Limits on regulator capacity
patterns.plain: A bill that bans a regulator from using its own testing tools, requires it to rely on outside assessors or sets low pay scales can reduce the regulator's own ability to evaluate.
patterns.fix: Authorize the regulator to build its own testing capacity and set competitive pay.
patterns.check: Find limits on the regulator's staffing, tools, pay and contracting. Ask whether it can test or investigate by itself, or must rely on the regulated party or paid third parties.
patterns.ex_ai: Barring internal testing tools, requiring third-party assessments or low pay scales reduces the regulator's own ability to evaluate.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on building inspections could require agencies to accept private inspector reports and bar them from buying testing equipment.

patterns.name: Reports and studies instead of action
headings: Reporting Requirements as Substitutes for Action
patterns.plain: Requiring a study or report in place of a concrete outcome can look like progress while the action itself is put off.
patterns.fix: Attach an action or default rule to each report and set deadlines.
patterns.check: Find each study, report or assessment. Ask what action follows it, by when, and whether the outcome changes anything if the report is late or never written.

patterns.name: Sequential studies
patterns.plain: When assessments are chained together, each with its own timeline, comment period and challenge, implementation is always waiting for one more study.
patterns.fix: Limit the process to one study with a deadline and an automatic next step.
patterns.check: Trace chains of studies where one report leads to another. Ask whether the text sets an end point, and what happens automatically when the last report is delivered.

patterns.name: Transparency defined thinly
patterns.plain: A bare notice that something exists or applies is less informative than disclosing how it works and its limits, and a law can require only the bare notice.
patterns.fix: Specify the content of disclosures, including limits and known risks, and who receives them.
patterns.check: Find what exactly must be disclosed and to whom. Ask whether the disclosure lets a reader judge quality, risks and limits, or only confirms that a thing exists.
patterns.ex_ai: A bare statement that content is AI-generated is less informative than disclosing training data and limitations, and laws can require only the bare statement.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a financial product bill could require a notice that fees apply without listing the amounts or when they are charged.

patterns.name: Labeling treated as the whole solution
patterns.plain: Labeling is inexpensive and may have little effect on what people believe or do, but can be treated as sufficient in place of structural measures.
patterns.fix: Pair labels with substantive duties and test whether the labels work.
patterns.check: Find where a label, notice or watermark is the only duty. Ask what evidence shows it changes behavior and what happens when it is ignored, removed or unseen.
patterns.ex_ai: Labeling is inexpensive and may have little effect on belief, but can be treated as sufficient in place of structural measures.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on sugary drinks might require only a warning label and no limit on marketing to children.

patterns.name: Control of evidence
patterns.plain: The records needed to show a violation are held by the party being regulated, so without disclosure, subpoena or preservation powers, enforcers and injured people may be unable to prove a case.
patterns.fix: Add disclosure, subpoena and record preservation powers for enforcers and claimants.
patterns.check: Find who holds the evidence needed to prove a violation. Ask whether the text gives enforcers and private parties access, subpoena power and a duty to preserve records, or leaves proof to the regulated party.
patterns.ex_ai: Companies hold the data needed to prove harm, and without disclosure powers, subpoena authority or preservation duties, regulators and plaintiffs cannot get it.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A workplace safety law might rely on employer inspection logs while giving inspectors no power to compel them.

patterns.name: Record retention missing
headings: Destroying the Evidentiary Trail by Design
patterns.plain: Without a duty to keep records, a party can minimize what it logs, which makes later review and accountability difficult.
patterns.fix: Require creation and retention of defined records for a set period, with access for enforcers.
patterns.check: Find duties to keep logs or records. Ask whether a retention period, content and format are set, who can access them, and whether a party could avoid creating the records at all.
patterns.ex_ai: Without record retention duties, systems can minimize logging, which makes later accountability difficult.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A food safety rule might require tests but no storage of results, so past outbreaks cannot be traced.

patterns.name: Researcher and journalist access
patterns.plain: Without access rights written into law, independent study of an industry depends on the goodwill of companies, which they can withdraw.
patterns.fix: Create a legal access right for vetted researchers, with protection from liability for good-faith work.
patterns.check: Check whether outside researchers, auditors and journalists have a legal right to data or facilities. Ask who qualifies, who can refuse, and whether good-faith research is protected from legal threats.
patterns.ex_ai: Without access rights written into law, independent evaluation depends on the goodwill of companies, which they can withdraw.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on hospital pricing could require posting prices but give researchers no right to the underlying billing data.

patterns.name: Missing whistleblower protection
patterns.plain: Employees are a likely source of information about problems, and without legal protection they can be silenced or penalized for speaking.
patterns.fix: Add anti-retaliation protection, confidential reporting channels and a remedy for retaliation.
patterns.check: Check whether the law protects people who report violations, including from retaliation, and whether it provides a safe channel. Ask who is covered, what remedy exists and who enforces it.
patterns.ex_ai: Employees are a likely source of safety information, and without protection they can be silenced or penalized.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on food plant safety might create inspection duties but offer no protection for workers who report violations.

patterns.name: Confidentiality agreements limit reporting
patterns.plain: If nondisclosure agreements stay fully enforceable, or exceptions apply only to confidential official channels, people may be unable to report concerns.
patterns.fix: Declare void any agreement terms that bar lawful reporting, and allow reports to regulators and others.
patterns.check: Find how the law treats confidentiality agreements. Ask whether they can block reports to regulators or the public, and whether the exception covers more than one confidential channel.
patterns.ex_ai: If nondisclosure agreements stay fully enforceable, or exceptions apply only to confidential regulatory channels, employees may be unable to report safety concerns.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on nursing home care might protect reports to the state agency but leave non-disparagement clauses enforceable against talking to families.

patterns.name: Audit frequency and scope
patterns.plain: Audits that are infrequent or narrow in scope can miss problems that develop between reviews or fall outside the items examined.
patterns.fix: Set review frequency by risk, include reviews triggered by changes, and define full scope and auditor independence.
patterns.check: Find audit or inspection duties. Ask how often they occur, what they cover, who performs them, and whether a fast changing product or practice could change between audits without being reviewed.
patterns.ex_ai: Annual or narrowly scoped audits miss fast-changing systems and misuse.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A building safety law might require one inspection every five years of listed items only, missing later repairs and unlisted hazards.

patterns.name: No records of input origin
headings: Training Data Provenance Requirements (or Lack Thereof)
patterns.plain: Without requirements to record where inputs came from, material of uncertain origin cannot be traced, and no one can be held responsible for its quality or legality.
patterns.fix: Require origin records for inputs, with retention periods and inspection rights.
patterns.check: Check whether the law requires records of the source of inputs, materials or data. Ask who keeps them, how long, and who can inspect them.
patterns.ex_ai: Without provenance requirements, training data of uncertain origin cannot be traced, and no one can be held responsible for the inputs.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on imported seafood could set quality rules but not require records of where the catch originated.

patterns.name: Retention versus deletion tension
patterns.plain: A duty to keep records for accountability can conflict with a duty to delete data for privacy, and a party can cite whichever duty is more convenient.
patterns.fix: State which duty prevails in each case and set retention periods with exceptions for audits.
patterns.check: Find duties to keep records and duties to delete data. Ask which prevails when they conflict, who decides, and whether a retention period is stated.
patterns.ex_ai: A duty to keep records for accountability can conflict with a duty to delete data for privacy, and a party can cite whichever duty is more convenient.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill requiring both audit logs and prompt deletion of customer data might let a firm cite either to avoid producing records.

patterns.name: Reported but not published
headings: What Must Be Reported Versus What Must Be Published
patterns.plain: Reports sent to regulators without public release keep the public from applying pressure on firms or comparing them.
patterns.fix: Require public release of reports in summary form or with sensitive parts blacked out, with narrow grounds for confidentiality.
patterns.check: Find each reporting duty and who receives the report. Ask whether it is published, in what form, how soon, and who may keep it confidential.
patterns.ex_ai: Reports sent to regulators without public release keep the public from applying pressure on companies or comparing them.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on school safety incidents might require reports to a state office but exempt them from public records requests.

patterns.name: Reports that cannot be compared
patterns.plain: When each regulated party chooses its own reporting format or method, the resulting data cannot be compared, so patterns across all regulated parties stay hidden.
patterns.fix: Require a standard template, defined metrics and a common method for all reporters.
patterns.check: Find reporting duties. Ask whether the text fixes a common template, metrics and method, or lets each reporter choose, and whether results could be compared across parties and years.
patterns.ex_ai: Reporting formats that differ between companies produce data that cannot be meaningfully compared.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A school discipline reporting law might let each district define its own categories, so statewide totals cannot be compared.

patterns.name: Reporting too infrequent
patterns.plain: Annual reporting for things that change quickly means the information is always out of date by the time it is seen.
patterns.fix: Set report frequency to the pace of change and add prompt notice of serious events.
patterns.check: Find how often reports are due and how long after the period they are published. Ask how fast the subject changes and whether serious events must be reported sooner.
patterns.ex_ai: Annual reporting for systems that change weekly means information is always outdated.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on wildfire risk equipment might require a yearly report though conditions change within days.

patterns.name: Severability used strategically
patterns.plain: A severability clause, which keeps the rest of a law in force if a court strikes down part of it, can preserve less visible provisions, while omitting one can make challenges to the whole law riskier or safer.
cues: if any provision of this act
patterns.fix: Include a clear severability clause and consider which provisions are essential.
patterns.check: Read the severability clause, or note its absence. Ask which provisions would survive if others were struck down, and whether the remainder still works as intended.

patterns.name: Savings clause without substance
patterns.plain: A clause preserving existing rights can have no practical effect if the new framework makes those rights hard to use in practice.
cues: nothing in this act shall be construed
shall not be construed to diminish
patterns.fix: Support the savings clause with rules that take effect and keep the rights usable.
patterns.check: Read each clause saying the Act does not affect existing rights. Ask whether other provisions make those rights harder to use in practice, such as through procedure, forum or proof rules.

patterns.name: Preemption of tort and common law
headings: Strategic Silence on Preemption of Common Law Claims
patterns.plain: Silence on state common law claims, or a freeze on new state rules, can leave doubt over whether courts may develop liability theories.
patterns.fix: State whether state tort and common law claims are preserved.
patterns.check: Search for language on state common law, tort claims or a bar on new state rules. Ask whether existing claims are preserved, and whether loose words such as 'requirements' could be read to eliminate them.
patterns.ex_ai: AI bills can leave doubt over whether state tort claims survive, or can freeze state legal frameworks for AI.

patterns.name: Repeal by conflicting later law
headings: Constructive Repeal Through Irreconcilable Later Enactment
patterns.plain: A later statute that is hard to reconcile with an earlier one leaves both in force, which creates uncertainty that only litigation can settle.
patterns.fix: Repeal or amend the earlier provisions expressly.
patterns.check: Compare the new provisions with earlier laws on the same subject. Ask whether any conflict exists, and whether the text repeals or amends the earlier provision expressly instead of leaving courts to reconcile them.

patterns.name: Placement within the code
headings: Strategic Placement Within the U.S. Code
patterns.plain: Where a provision is codified (placed in the permanent legal code) affects which agency runs it, which committees oversee it and which precedents apply.
patterns.fix: Choose a placement that fits the intended regime and agency, and state it in the bill.
patterns.check: Check where each provision is to be codified. Ask which agency, committee and body of precedent that location brings, and whether the placement matches the regime the bill describes.

patterns.name: Interaction with an existing liability shield
patterns.plain: Whether a new activity counts as publishing or neutral hosting under an existing immunity can be unresolved, and the bill may be silent on it.
patterns.fix: State whether the existing shield applies to the new conduct and, if so, with what limits.
patterns.check: Find any existing law that shields a class of actors from liability. Ask whether the bill says if it applies to the new activity, and who decides if the text is silent.
patterns.ex_ai: Whether algorithmic curation counts as publishing or neutral hosting is unresolved, and the bill may be silent on it.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill creating duties for ride platforms might not say whether an older liability shield for intermediaries still applies.

patterns.name: Output as original work (AI outputs)
patterns.plain: Treating AI outputs as original works can reduce the bargaining power of rights holders over the use of their work for training.
patterns.fix: Address training use and output ownership expressly in the text.
patterns.check: Find how the bill treats ownership of machine-generated output and the use of existing works as input. Ask whether the people whose works were used have any claim or notice.
patterns.ex_ai: Treating AI outputs as original works can reduce the bargaining power of rights holders over the use of their work for training.

patterns.name: Narrow standard displaces stronger law
patterns.plain: A new, weaker standard on a topic can displace stronger claims under existing civil rights or consumer laws if the text is not clear about overlap.
patterns.fix: State that existing rights and remedies remain, and that compliance here does not excuse compliance elsewhere.
patterns.check: Find language on preemption (where one law overrides another), supremacy and savings. Ask whether existing rights and remedies survive, and whether compliance with the new law is treated as compliance with older ones.
patterns.ex_ai: Weaker AI-specific standards may displace stronger claims under existing civil rights laws.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on tenant screening could set a mild fairness test and be read to replace stronger claims under housing law.

patterns.name: Intellectual property shields from inspection
patterns.plain: Patents, copyright and trade secret protection can limit outside inspection and competition, which may block audits or reuse that the law otherwise expects.
patterns.fix: Provide confidential access for regulators and auditors that overrides trade secret objections.
patterns.check: Find disclosure and inspection duties. Ask whether trade secret or other intellectual property claims can block access, and whether confidential review by auditors or regulators is guaranteed.
patterns.ex_ai: Patents, copyrightable outputs and trade secret model weights together can limit auditing and competition.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A drug pricing law might require cost disclosure but let firms withhold figures as trade secrets.

patterns.name: Contract terms override public law
patterns.plain: Without a ban on waiving rights, standard form contracts can set aside protections the statute gives, so the protection depends on what a party signs.
patterns.fix: Add an anti-waiver clause and treat contrary terms as void.
patterns.check: Find any rights or duties stated as defaults. Ask whether a contract, waiver or agreement can alter them, and whether the text says protections cannot be waived.
patterns.ex_ai: Without anti-waiver provisions, contracts of adhesion (take-it-or-leave-it contracts) can set aside protections the statute gives.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A tenant rights bill might not say lease terms cannot waive repair duties, so landlords can add a standard waiver.

patterns.name: Authority open to major questions challenge
patterns.plain: Grants of authority that are just ambiguous enough to be challenged under the major questions doctrine can face years of litigation.
patterns.fix: State the authority and its limits clearly, with specific findings on scope.
patterns.check: Find grants of authority over matters of large economic or social reach. Ask whether the text states the power and its limits plainly, or relies on general words a court could find too thin.

patterns.name: Ambiguity after Chevron
patterns.plain: Now that courts no longer defer to agency readings of unclear law, vague language is resolved by courts, which can delay or reverse an agency's interpretation.
patterns.fix: Draft specifically or give express discretion to the agency.
patterns.check: Identify provisions that rely on the agency's reading of an unclear term. Ask whether a court, deciding the term for itself, could reach a different meaning, and whether the text states the agency's discretion expressly.

patterns.name: Findings sections and constitutionality
headings: Strategic Use of "Findings" Sections to Manufacture Deference
patterns.plain: Congressional findings shape how courts judge whether a law is constitutional, and findings that are well drafted or weakened change how open the law is to challenge.
patterns.fix: Include specific findings supported by record evidence.
patterns.check: Read the findings against the powers the bill uses. Ask whether they state specific facts tied to each power, and whether a court could use them or their absence to judge validity.

patterns.name: Legislative veto provisions
patterns.plain: Legislative veto provisions are unenforceable, but agencies often comply anyway, which gives Congress control through political norms.
patterns.fix: Use joint resolutions that must be presented to the President instead of one-house vetoes.
patterns.check: Find provisions letting one chamber or a committee block or approve an agency action. Ask whether the action must pass through the ordinary lawmaking process, and what happens if the agency ignores the veto.

patterns.name: Provisions exposed to speech challenge
headings: Designing Provisions to Fail First Amendment Challenges
patterns.plain: A slightly overbroad provision can be struck down by a court on speech grounds, and the ruling can narrow what later laws are able to do.
patterns.fix: Tailor provisions narrowly, state the interest, add severability and avoid needless content based triggers.
patterns.check: Find provisions that restrict or compel communication. Ask whether they are tailored to a stated interest, whether they are open to a speech challenge, and what a loss would mean for the rest of the law.
patterns.ex_ai: Slightly overbroad provisions may be struck down, and the resulting decision can limit what regulators can do for many years.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A disclosure law might compel detailed statements from any publisher, inviting a challenge that sets a broad precedent.

patterns.name: Takings exposure
patterns.plain: Provisions that compel sharing or access to property can draw takings challenges (claims that the government took property without payment) that could limit regulation of whole categories.
patterns.fix: Provide compensation or narrow the compelled access, and include fallback provisions if challenged.
patterns.check: Find any duty that forces a party to share, license or give access to assets. Ask whether compensation is addressed and whether a challenge could strike the broader scheme.
patterns.ex_ai: Data sharing or forced access provisions can draw takings challenges that could limit regulation of whole categories.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill forcing utilities to open private lines to competitors could be challenged for lack of compensation.

patterns.name: Due process vulnerability
patterns.plain: Strong procedures paired with vague standards can invite due process challenges that remove enforcement while the law stays in force.
patterns.fix: Pair strong powers with clear standards, notice, hearing and appeal rights.
patterns.check: Find enforcement powers and the standards they apply. Ask whether affected parties get fair notice, a hearing and a clear rule, or whether vagueness leaves the power open to challenge.
patterns.ex_ai: Aggressive procedures with vague standards invite due process challenges that can remove enforcement while leaving the law in place.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A licensing law might allow immediate suspension for conduct harmful to the public, with no defined test or hearing.

patterns.name: Exposure to structural legal challenge
patterns.plain: A provision that may conflict with limits on the enacting body's power can attract litigation, and the result or the threat of it can support arguments for a weaker uniform standard.
patterns.fix: Tie reach to local effects, add findings and severability, and avoid needless extraterritorial reach.
patterns.check: Find provisions that reach beyond the enacting body's territory or powers. Ask whether they are open to a structural legal challenge and what a loss would do to the rest of the law.
patterns.ex_ai: Vulnerable state laws can generate litigation that supports arguments for a weaker federal standard.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A state labeling law might regulate out of state sales, drawing a challenge that ends in a weaker national standard.

patterns.name: Sense of Congress language
headings: Sense of Congress Resolutions Masquerading as Action
patterns.plain: A sense of Congress statement has no legal force but can be presented as if Congress took a position.
patterns.fix: Replace it with a provision that creates a legal duty, or remove it.
patterns.check: Find statements of the legislature's sense or encouragement. Ask whether any operative duty follows, and whether the statement could be presented as a legal position.

patterns.name: Preamble goals without operative force
patterns.plain: A preamble declares bold goals while the provisions that create legal duties contain qualifications that keep the goals from being achieved.
cues: it is the policy of the united states
patterns.fix: Align operative text with each stated goal and state that purposes guide interpretation.
patterns.check: Set each goal in the purposes or findings beside the operative sections. Ask whether any qualifier, exemption or discretion in the operative text can keep that goal from being met, and whether purposes guide interpretation.

patterns.name: Competitiveness findings
patterns.plain: Findings that regulation could cause a country to fall behind others can be cited later in rulemaking and cost-benefit analysis, which can change how the operative rules are read.
patterns.fix: Keep findings balanced and state that they do not limit protective duties.
patterns.check: Find findings or purpose statements about competitiveness, growth or leadership. Ask whether they are tied to operative text and could be used to narrow duties or justify exemptions.
patterns.ex_ai: Findings that regulation could cause the country to fall behind competitors can shape later rulemaking and cost-benefit analysis.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A telecom bill might include a finding that regulation threatens leadership, later cited to justify weaker rules.

patterns.name: Voluntary commitments as substitute
patterns.plain: Voluntary pledges cited as proof that law is unnecessary can later be written into the law as its standard, so the legal standard is low.
patterns.fix: Set the standard in the statute, with voluntary measures counting only as a minimum.
patterns.check: Find references to voluntary frameworks, pledges or best practices. Ask whether the law adopts them as its standard, who wrote them, and whether they are enforceable.
patterns.ex_ai: Voluntary pledges cited as proof that law is unnecessary can later be written into the law as its standard.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on data brokers might adopt an industry code of conduct as the legal safe harbor.

patterns.name: Characterization that assigns responsibility
patterns.plain: Describing a product as a mere tool, or by another label, can limit the responsibility of its maker and block rules suited to how it actually behaves.
patterns.fix: Attach duties to function and effect rather than to a descriptive label.
patterns.check: Find labels that describe what a thing is, such as tool, aid or assistant. Ask what legal consequences follow from the label, and whether the actual behavior fits.
patterns.ex_ai: Describing AI as a tool can limit responsibility and block rules suited to autonomous systems.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on automated trading might call software a mere tool of the trader, so the maker faces no duty when it acts unexpectedly.

patterns.name: Harm treated as a fixable defect
headings: Embedding the "Bias Is a Bug" Frame
Embedding the "Bias Is a Bug, Not a Feature" Frame
patterns.plain: Describing a harm as a technical defect to be improved can make the only remedy an improvement by the operator, rather than a limit on where or whether the product is used.
patterns.fix: Provide limits on use and remedies independent of whether the operator claims to have improved the product.
patterns.check: Find language that treats a harm as an error rate or defect. Ask whether the only remedy is improvement, and whether use can be limited, paused or prohibited if the defect persists.
patterns.ex_ai: Framing bias as a technical defect makes the remedy an improvement to the system rather than a limit on its use.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A lending bill might require lenders to refine scoring methods after disparities appear, with no ability to restrict the method itself.

patterns.name: Nominal human review
patterns.plain: A requirement for human review can create the appearance of oversight when the reviewer lacks time, information or authority to depart from the recommended result.
patterns.fix: Define meaningful review, give reviewers authority and time, and track how often reviewers overrule the recommendation.
patterns.check: Find required human review or sign-off. Ask whether the reviewer has the time, training, information and power to disagree, and whether outcomes show how often they do.
patterns.ex_ai: A human review requirement can create the appearance of oversight when reviewers tend to accept the system's output.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A loan rule might require an officer to sign each decision, though the officer has seconds per file and rarely overrules the score.

patterns.name: Assistance that does not assist
patterns.plain: Support programs that are underfunded, mismatched to need or hard to qualify for can look like a response to harm while reaching few of the people affected.
patterns.fix: Fund assistance to match expected need and set simple eligibility and outcome reporting.
patterns.check: Find support or transition programs. Ask what funding, eligibility rules and application steps apply, how many people could realistically qualify, and whether the support matches the loss.
patterns.ex_ai: Retraining or support programs that are underfunded, mismatched or hard to qualify for give the appearance of addressing displacement.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A plant closure law might offer retraining for jobs that do not exist locally, with enrollment limited to a small number of workers.

patterns.name: Assessments without effect
patterns.plain: Assessments that only inform, and do not affect whether or how something goes ahead, show people the harm while the project proceeds unchanged.
patterns.fix: Tie assessment findings to conditions, mitigation duties or review before the activity proceeds.
patterns.check: Find required assessments or statements. Ask whether any finding can delay, change or stop the activity, who can act on it, and whether the public can respond.
patterns.ex_ai: Informational assessments that do not affect deployment decisions show communities their harm while deployment goes ahead.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A development law might require a community impact report that expressly cannot delay a building permit.

patterns.name: Rival framing of restraint
headings: The "Adversary Will Do It Anyway" Argument
patterns.plain: Presenting each protective rule as helping a competitor or rival can make restraint look like a loss and can displace safeguards, even where the claim is untested.
patterns.fix: Require stated evidence for competitive claims and keep protective duties independent of them.
patterns.check: Find statements that tie a safeguard to advantage for a rival nation, firm or sector. Ask what evidence supports the claim and whether the safeguard still operates independently of it.
patterns.ex_ai: Framing every safety rule as helping a rival nation presents restraint as giving up an advantage and can displace safety measures.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A food import safety bill might be opposed on the ground that stricter inspection would give business to foreign suppliers.

patterns.name: Compliance costs favor incumbents
patterns.plain: Heavy compliance requirements can act as barriers that large firms absorb and smaller or community competitors cannot, so a safeguard can also reduce competition.
patterns.fix: Scale duties to size and risk and provide support or simplified paths for small actors.
patterns.check: Find registration, licensing and compliance program duties. Ask what they cost, whether small actors can meet them, and whether duties scale with size and risk.
patterns.ex_ai: Heavy compliance requirements can act as barriers that large firms can absorb and smaller or open source competitors cannot.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A food safety bill might require a full time compliance officer, which a small producer cannot afford.

patterns.name: Rules that entrench existing holders
headings: Data Moat Protection Through Privacy Framing
patterns.plain: Limits on gathering new resources can leave established firms with what they already hold while newcomers start with nothing, so a protective rule can also reduce competition.
patterns.fix: Apply restrictions to existing holdings in a comparable way or give entrants access to shared inputs.
patterns.check: Find rules that restrict collecting or acquiring an input. Ask whether existing holders keep their stock, whether entrants face the full restriction, and how the effect on competition was weighed.
patterns.ex_ai: Privacy rules limiting new collection can leave established firms with historic data while new entrants have none.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A licensing rule closing new permits for a resource might leave early permit holders with all of the supply.

patterns.name: Thresholds tied to an aging proxy
patterns.plain: A threshold set in a technical measure can stop tracking the real risk as technology changes, and can bind only the largest actors while leaving similar risks uncovered.
patterns.fix: Pair thresholds with a risk based test and an update process, and add anti-evasion language.
patterns.check: Find every numeric threshold. Ask what it is measured in, whether that measure will still track the risk in five years, and whether an actor can stay just under it.
patterns.ex_ai: Thresholds set to capture only the largest labs impose costs that only well-resourced firms can handle and leave others unregulated.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A chemical plant safety law might apply by storage volume of one substance, missing equally dangerous plants using a substitute.

patterns.name: Rules attached to one access point
headings: API Access as a Regulatory Chokepoint
patterns.plain: Placing duties on whoever controls a single access point can give that party the power to decide who gets access, and can shape or end other ways the product is distributed.
patterns.fix: State what the access point holder must and need not do, and protect lawful alternative routes.
patterns.check: Find the point in the supply or access chain where duties attach. Ask who controls it, what the duty gives them power to refuse, and what other distribution routes the rule affects.
patterns.ex_ai: Rules at the API level give API controllers the power to decide who gets access, and can end open source distribution.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A pharmacy law might place all dispensing duties on wholesalers, giving them power over which small pharmacies can stock a drug.

patterns.name: Government purchasing as standard-setting
headings: Government Procurement as De Facto Standard-Setting
patterns.plain: Public purchasing rules can effectively set industry standards with little public scrutiny and can favor incumbents.
patterns.fix: Open purchasing standards to public comment and set them to match the law's goals.
patterns.check: Find rules on government purchasing, contracts or acquisition that set requirements. Ask who writes them, whether the public can comment, and whether they favor firms already in the market.
patterns.ex_ai: Federal procurement rules effectively set industry standards with little public scrutiny and can favor incumbents.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on school technology could set purchasing requirements that only large vendors can meet.

patterns.name: Weak portability standards
patterns.plain: If moving data or accounts is hard or limited, switching costs remain high, so the law can appear to promote competition while changing little.
patterns.fix: Require standard formats, full scope, timely transfer and ongoing access for the receiving party.
patterns.check: Find portability or transfer rights. Ask what format, scope and timing are required, whether the receiving party can use the result, and whether the right is enforceable in practice.
patterns.ex_ai: Weak portability standards preserve switching costs while seeming to promote competition.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A banking bill might let customers download statements as images, which cannot be loaded into another provider's system.

patterns.name: Interoperability mandates or absence
patterns.plain: Without interoperability, network effects can keep users tied to leading providers, so whether to require it is a decision about market structure.
patterns.fix: Require open, documented standards and access for competing providers.
patterns.check: Find whether systems must work with others. Ask what standards, access and timing apply, and whether silence leaves leading providers able to keep users in.
patterns.ex_ai: Without interoperability, network effects keep users tied to leading providers, so the choice is a market structure decision.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A payments bill might say nothing about connecting to other networks, leaving users tied to the largest one.

patterns.name: Rules on one layer favor integrated firms
patterns.plain: Rules applying to one layer of a supply chain favor firms that span several layers and can shift costs between them.
patterns.fix: Apply rules to the integrated firm as a whole or add rules on dealings between its units.
patterns.check: Map the layers of the industry and see which the rules cover. Ask whether a firm operating in several layers can move costs or activity to an uncovered one.
patterns.ex_ai: Rules applying to one layer favor integrated firms that can shift costs between layers.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a bill capping fees by pharmacies might not cover a firm that owns both the insurer and the pharmacy.

patterns.name: Review triggers that miss most deals
patterns.plain: Review triggers based on price or size can let most transactions pass unexamined, especially where the thing acquired has little or no sale price but large strategic value.
patterns.fix: Add review triggers based on factors such as users, data or capability, not price alone.
patterns.check: Find the trigger for review of a transaction or entry. Ask what it is measured in, whether low priced or free items can fall below it, and whether data, users or capability could be counted instead.
patterns.ex_ai: High thresholds or price-based tests, which often come to zero for free AI products, exempt most acquisitions.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A hospital merger review law might trigger only above a dollar value, so purchases of small clinics with large local market share fall outside it.

patterns.name: Narrow ban implying permission
patterns.plain: Prohibiting one specific act can be read as allowing closely related conduct that the text does not mention.
patterns.fix: Add a general prohibition and state that unlisted related conduct is not authorized.
patterns.check: Find prohibitions that name one specific act. Ask whether closely related conduct is left outside, and whether a general prohibition or a statement that unlisted conduct is not authorized is present.

patterns.name: Permit with no decision deadline
patterns.plain: A permit or approval requirement with no deadline for the agency lets applications wait indefinitely, so approval may never arrive.
patterns.fix: Set a decision deadline with automatic approval or a right to sue if it is missed.
patterns.check: Find each permit, license, approval or application step. Ask whether the agency has a decision deadline, and what happens to an applicant if it passes.

patterns.name: Conference committee rewrites
patterns.plain: Final text is reconciled by a small committee, so changes can occur with limited transparency after both chambers have debated.
patterns.fix: Require a waiting period and public posting of conference text before votes.
patterns.check: Compare the final text with the versions each chamber passed. Ask which provisions are new or changed, when the text was posted, and how long members had to read it before voting.

patterns.name: Signing statements
patterns.plain: Presidential statements on how ambiguous provisions will be read signal how the law will be enforced without a vote.
patterns.fix: Draft provisions specifically and monitor signing statements for their effect.
patterns.check: Compare the text with any statement by the signing official on how it will be read. Ask whether the statement narrows a provision, and whether the text settles the point itself.

patterns.name: Riders and omnibus bundling
patterns.plain: Unrelated provisions added to bills that Congress must pass receive little scrutiny and can change unrelated policy areas.
patterns.fix: Require amendments to relate to the bill's subject and set a posting period for large bills.
patterns.check: Look for provisions unrelated to the bill's main subject. Ask whether each has been separately debated, how much time readers had, and what unrelated policy it changes.

patterns.name: Retroactive redefinition
patterns.plain: A later law that clarifies an earlier one can reinterpret it in ways that conflict with original intent or settled court rulings.
cues: shall be deemed to have always
patterns.fix: Review later clarifying provisions against the original purpose and court readings.
patterns.check: Find provisions described as clarifying earlier law. Ask whether they change what the earlier law was read to mean, and whether they apply to events or cases already underway.

patterns.name: Staged legislative history
patterns.plain: Floor statements and reports can be prepared to narrow or contradict plain text, and courts sometimes consult them.
patterns.fix: Write the intended meaning into the text itself.
patterns.check: Compare the text with reports and floor statements about it. Ask whether any statement narrows or contradicts the words, and whether the intended meaning is written into the bill itself.

patterns.name: Enrolled bill doctrine
headings: The Enrolled Bill Doctrine as Cover
patterns.plain: Once signed, the enrolled text (the final signed version) is treated as conclusive even where it differs from what chambers voted on.
patterns.fix: Check enrolled text against passed text before signature.
patterns.check: Compare the signed text with the text each chamber passed. Ask whether any word differs, and who is responsible for confirming they match before signature.

patterns.name: Self-executing House rules
patterns.plain: A special procedural rule can deem a bill passed without a separate vote, which places policy in that rule and skips normal deliberation.
patterns.fix: Require separate recorded votes on substantive text.
patterns.check: Check whether a procedural rule deems the bill or text adopted. Ask whether members vote separately on the substance, and what policy the procedural measure contains.

patterns.name: Holman rule and targeted defunding
headings: The Holman Rule and Targeted Defunding
patterns.plain: Amendments to spending bills can reduce named employees' pay to one dollar, which stops enforcement without changing the statute.
patterns.fix: Protect enforcement positions through statute and track appropriations amendments.
patterns.check: Check appropriations text for limits on pay or positions of named people or offices. Ask whether the limit could stop a duty from being carried out while the statute stays unchanged.

patterns.name: Technical corrections used for substance
patterns.plain: Bills presented as fixing typos can make substantive changes that receive little scrutiny.
patterns.fix: Limit technical corrections to enumerated typographic fixes with review.
patterns.check: Read each section labeled technical or conforming. Ask whether any change alters who is covered, what is required or how much money is involved, beyond fixing errors.

patterns.name: Congressional Review Act timing
headings: Drafting to Exploit the Congressional Review Act Window
patterns.plain: Rules finalized late in an administration can be repealed by the next Congress, and how a bill is drafted affects how quickly rules can be finished.
patterns.fix: Set deadlines that allow rules to be finalized outside the review window.
patterns.check: Check the dates by which rules must be issued. Ask whether finalizing them near the end of an administration leaves them open to disapproval by the next legislature.

patterns.name: Committee assignment shapes the bill
patterns.plain: The committee a bill is sent to sets the expertise, priorities and interests that shape its text, so the choice of committee can influence the result.
patterns.fix: Provide joint or sequential referral to bodies with relevant expertise.
patterns.check: Identify which committee or body drafted or reviewed the bill. Ask whether its jurisdiction fits the subject, which other bodies had a claim, and how the choice of committee could have shaped the wording.
patterns.ex_ai: Committee assignment determines the perspective from which a bill is written, so sending a bill to one committee over another shapes the result.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A bill on school food might go to a committee focused on agriculture, framing it around crop supply and not child nutrition.

patterns.name: Burdensome step that invites opposition
headings: Age Verification as a Poison Pill
patterns.plain: A required step that is costly, intrusive or hard to carry out can draw broad opposition that delays an otherwise supported bill, or can be hard to comply with in practice.
patterns.fix: Use a feasible, privacy protective version of the step and keep it severable from the core duties.
patterns.check: Find any required verification, registration or documentation step. Ask whether it is feasible, what it costs users and regulated parties, and whether its burden could draw opposition that endangers the whole law.
patterns.ex_ai: Requiring age verification that is infeasible or invasive can generate opposition that causes the whole bill to fail.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: A tenant protection bill might require landlords to collect proof of income from every applicant, drawing objections that take attention away from its main protections.

patterns.name: Complexity that hides the operative rule
patterns.plain: Text so long, layered or cross-referenced that few readers can find what it does can let a significant provision pass without scrutiny.
patterns.fix: State each operative rule in one place, limit nested cross-references, and supply a section-by-section summary that matches the text.
patterns.check: Count the cross-references and nested exceptions a reader must follow to learn what one provision does. Ask whether the operative rule could be stated in one place.
patterns.ex_ai: Submitting thousands of pages of technical documentation can obscure information through volume.
patterns.ex_other: For illustration: a benefits bill might state its eligibility rule in a way that can only be found by reading four sections and two other statutes together.

patterns.name: Modifier scope after a list
patterns.plain: A qualifying phrase before or after a list can be read as applying to the nearest item or to every item.
patterns.fix: Restructure the list into separate subparagraphs or repeat the modifier so its reach is explicit.
patterns.check: Find each qualifying phrase placed before or after a list. Ask whether it applies to the nearest item or to every item, and whether a reasonable reader could pick either.

patterns.name: "And" and "or" in conditions and negations
patterns.plain: A list of conditions joined by "and" or "or", especially under a negative, can be read as requiring all or any one.
patterns.fix: Use 'all of the following' or 'any of the following', and set conditions out as separate lettered items.
patterns.check: Find lists of conditions joined by 'and' or 'or', especially under 'not' or 'no'. Ask whether the text requires all conditions or any one, and whether the reverse reading would change the result.

patterns.name: Punctuation-dependent meaning
patterns.plain: The scope of a provision depends on whether a comma is present.
patterns.fix: Recast the sentence so its meaning does not depend on a comma, using separate clauses or subparagraphs.
patterns.check: Find sentences where a comma or its absence changes who or what is covered. Ask what the sentence means with the punctuation removed, and whether another reading is plausible.

patterns.name: Article and number choice
patterns.plain: "A", "the" or a plural leaves open whether one item or several, or one document or several, satisfies the rule.
patterns.fix: State the number required, such as 'at least one' or 'each', instead of relying on articles or plurals.
patterns.check: Find uses of 'a', 'the' or plural forms in duties and tests. Ask whether one item or several satisfies the rule, and whether one document, person or act is meant.

patterns.name: Tense that leaves earlier conduct in doubt
patterns.plain: A provision not written in the present tense leaves unclear whether it reaches conduct before enactment.
patterns.fix: Write operative provisions in the present tense and state expressly whether earlier conduct is covered.
patterns.check: Find verbs in the past or future tense in operative provisions. Ask whether the provision reaches conduct before enactment, and whether the text says so.

patterns.name: Duty with no named actor
patterns.plain: A passive sentence states that something "shall be done" without saying who must do it.
patterns.fix: Name the responsible official or body in each duty, and state the consequence of not acting.
patterns.check: Find passive sentences saying something 'shall be done'. For each, ask who must do it, and who answers if it is not done.

patterns.name: "Shall" used to state a rule
patterns.plain: "Shall" appears where no one has a duty, which blurs the difference between commands and statements of fact.
patterns.fix: Use 'is' or 'has' for statements of status and reserve 'shall' for duties with a named actor.
patterns.src: ULC rule 203(e) as quoted by MTC
patterns.check: Find uses of 'shall' where no person has a duty, such as statements of status or effect. Ask whether a command or a declaration is meant.

patterns.name: Prohibition silent on acts done in violation
patterns.plain: A "shall not" or "may not" does not say whether an act done in violation is void.
patterns.fix: State the legal effect of an act done in violation, such as that it is void or voidable, and who may raise it.
patterns.check: Find each 'shall not' or 'may not' and ask whether an act done in violation is void, voidable or valid. Ask who can challenge it.

patterns.name: Proviso of uncertain reach
patterns.plain: "Provided that" language leaves unclear whether it sets a condition, an exception or a new rule, and which words it attaches to.
patterns.fix: Replace the proviso with a separate sentence or subsection stating whether it is a condition, an exception or a rule.
patterns.check: Find each 'provided that' clause. Ask whether it sets a condition, an exception or a new rule, and which words it attaches to.

patterns.name: Varying words for one thing
patterns.plain: Different words for the same idea, or one word in two senses, invite a court to presume different meanings.
patterns.fix: Use one term for one idea throughout and define it once.
patterns.check: Compare the words used for the same idea across sections. Ask whether a court could presume different meanings, and whether one word is used in two senses.

patterns.name: Surplus words
patterns.plain: Redundant words or doublets (paired words with nearly the same meaning) let a party argue that a broad reading makes another clause meaningless.
patterns.fix: Delete redundant words, or state that paired terms are to be read together.
patterns.check: Find doublets and repeated phrases such as 'rules and regulations'. Ask whether a party could argue a broad reading makes another clause meaningless, or that each word must add something.

patterns.name: Time computation gaps
patterns.plain: "Within", "before" and "after" can leave unclear when a period starts or whether the named date itself counts.
patterns.fix: State the start event, the end date and whether both are included, and how weekends and holidays are treated.
patterns.check: Find each 'within', 'before' and 'after' period. Ask when the period starts, whether the named date itself is included, and who decides if the start is unclear.

patterns.name: Condition placed in one subpart
patterns.plain: Text inside one subparagraph, or flush text after a list, leaves unclear which of the parallel provisions it governs.
patterns.fix: Move the condition into its own provision or repeat it in each parallel provision it governs.
patterns.src: UK drafting guidance, Part 3.6; CRS R45153
patterns.check: Find text inside one subparagraph or flush text after a list. Ask which of the parallel provisions it governs, and whether the layout answers that.

patterns.name: "Deem" used for a judgment
patterns.plain: "Deems" is used for an exercise of judgment instead of a legal fiction, which is a rule treating something as true, leaving the standard unclear.
patterns.fix: Use 'deemed' only for legal fictions and state the standard where an official must judge.
patterns.check: Find each use of 'deem' or 'deemed'. Ask whether a legal fiction is meant or an exercise of judgment, and what standard guides the decision.

patterns.name: Drafting slip with substantive effect
patterns.plain: A wrong cross-reference, an omitted item or a typographical error can change the result of applying the law.
patterns.fix: Verify every cross-reference and list against the text before enactment, and add a correction process for later errors.
patterns.check: Check cross-references, lists and numbers for wrong citations, omitted items and typographical errors. Ask whether correcting each would change who is covered or what is required.

patterns.name: Inconsistent base in parallel clauses
patterns.plain: Two parallel provisions calculate amounts from different bases, such as gross amounts in one and net amounts in the other.
patterns.fix: Define the base once and use it in each parallel clause.
patterns.check: Compare parallel provisions that compute amounts, such as gross against net. Ask whether the same base is used in each and whether the difference changes the result.

patterns.name: Unreconciled drafts within one act
patterns.plain: A phrase in one section does not fit the structure of the rest of a long act assembled from separate drafts.
patterns.fix: Run a conformity review of terms, definitions and structure across the whole text before enactment.
patterns.check: Read the long act for phrases that do not fit its overall structure or defined terms. Ask whether sections were drafted separately and whether they still agree.

patterns.name: Heading at odds with the text
patterns.plain: A short title, heading or slogan describes more or less than the operative words do.
patterns.fix: Make headings accurate descriptions, and state that headings do not affect meaning.
patterns.check: Compare each title, heading or slogan with the operative words beneath it. Ask whether it describes more or less than the text does.

patterns.name: Bill-text length that hides the rule
patterns.plain: Excess length and nesting make the operative rule, meaning the part that creates the duty, hard to find.
patterns.fix: Move the core rule to a short, early provision and reduce nesting.
patterns.check: Find the operative rule in the longest or most nested sections. Ask whether a reader can state it in one sentence, and how many cross-references are needed.

patterns.name: Canons available on both sides
patterns.plain: An ambiguous sentence can be argued under opposing canons (standard rules for reading legal text), so the outcome cannot be predicted from the text.
patterns.fix: Resolve the ambiguity in the text and add a construction rule stating the intended breadth.
patterns.check: Find ambiguous sentences and ask which interpretive canons each side could cite. Ask whether the outcome could be predicted from the text alone.

patterns.name: "Means" where an open list was intended
patterns.plain: A definition uses "means", which makes the list complete, although the drafter intended it to give only examples.
patterns.fix: Use 'includes' for examples and reserve 'means' for exhaustive definitions.
patterns.check: Find definitions beginning 'means' and ask whether the list is meant to be exhaustive. Ask whether examples were intended and later items could be left out.

patterns.name: Operative rule inside a definition
patterns.plain: A duty, exception or condition is placed in a definition, where readers and the people who organize the legal code do not expect it.
patterns.fix: Move operative content into the operative sections and keep definitions to meaning only.
patterns.check: Read definitions for duties, exceptions or conditions. Ask whether a reader looking at the operative sections would find them there.

patterns.name: Context-escape wording in a definition
patterns.plain: "Unless the context requires otherwise" lets the defined meaning be set aside case by case.
patterns.fix: Delete the clause or list the specific contexts where a different meaning applies.
patterns.check: Find 'unless the context requires otherwise' in a definition. Ask who decides when the context differs, and where the defined meaning could be set aside.

patterns.name: Defined term far from ordinary meaning
patterns.plain: A defined label is given a meaning that departs from common usage, or the label is too bland to signal what it covers.
patterns.fix: Use a label that reflects the content of the definition, or avoid reusing an ordinary word with a special meaning.
patterns.check: Compare each defined term with its everyday meaning. Ask whether the label misleads, or is too bland to signal what it covers.

patterns.name: Reliance on Dictionary Act defaults
patterns.plain: The bill silently relies on, or conflicts with, the default definitions in Title 1 of the United States Code, such as "person" including corporations.
patterns.fix: Define key terms in the bill instead of relying on general defaults, or state which default applies.
patterns.check: Find terms such as 'person' that are not defined in the bill. Ask whether general default definitions apply, and whether they fit the bill's purpose.

patterns.name: Status label without a functional test
patterns.plain: Treatment turns on a label such as "limited partner" or "corporation" that a party can adopt without changing what it does.
patterns.fix: Add a functional test describing what the party does, alongside or in place of the label.
patterns.ex_ai: Workers managed by algorithms may not be legally recognized as employees, so employment protections do not apply to them.
patterns.check: Find rules that turn on a status label. Ask whether a party could adopt the label without changing what it does, and whether a functional test is present.

patterns.name: Definition bound to older technology
patterns.plain: An element or definition describes the technology of its day and does not fit what replaced it.
patterns.fix: Define by function rather than by method, and give a body authority to update the definition.
patterns.src: Facebook v. Duguid; Levy and Narechania
patterns.check: Find definitions that describe a specific method, device or medium. Ask whether a replacement technology would fall outside, and who can update the definition.

patterns.name: Definition that sweeps in bystanders
patterns.plain: A definition is broad enough to reach people or everyday conduct outside the stated aim, with limits left to official assurance or prosecutorial choice.
patterns.fix: Add express exclusions and a purpose or intent element so the definition reaches only the intended conduct.
patterns.check: Test each broad definition against everyday conduct outside the bill's aim. Ask whether limits rest on official assurance rather than text.

patterns.name: General term beyond expected applications
patterns.plain: A broad word reaches cases the enacting legislature did not foresee.
patterns.fix: State the purpose in the text and add a rule on how courts should treat cases outside the expected applications.
patterns.check: Find broad words and ask what cases the drafters did not foresee. Ask whether the outcome in those cases fits the purpose.

patterns.name: Two scopes within one bill
patterns.plain: Different sections of the same bill define the covered class differently.
patterns.fix: Define the covered class once and use that term in every section.
patterns.check: Compare how each section describes the covered class. Ask whether they differ, and which one governs where they conflict.

patterns.name: Terms inconsistent with the amended statute
patterns.plain: Inserted text uses words that mean something different in the statute it amends or in a neighboring one.
patterns.fix: Conform inserted terms to the amended statute, or define them for the inserted text.
patterns.src: EU Joint Practical Guide, guideline 6; HOLC Guide
patterns.check: Compare inserted words with the same words in the statute being amended and neighboring statutes. Ask whether they carry different meanings there.

patterns.name: Omitted case
patterns.plain: The text is silent on a category or situation, and courts treat the silence as deliberate.
patterns.fix: Add a catch-all or a statement of how omitted cases are treated, and name the cases that are meant to be left out.
patterns.check: List the categories and situations a reader would expect the text to address. Ask which are missing and whether a court could treat the silence as deliberate.

patterns.name: Bright line that invites design-around
patterns.plain: A rule is so specific that conduct just outside it escapes.
patterns.fix: Pair the bright line with an anti-avoidance rule and a power to adjust it by rule.
patterns.check: Find precise thresholds and cutoffs. Ask what conduct just outside them would escape, and whether the purpose is served by that result.

patterns.name: Self-determined coverage
patterns.plain: The regulated party decides whether it is covered, with no registry or record of the decision.
patterns.fix: Require registration or a written determination that the agency can inspect, and let the agency make its own coverage finding.
patterns.check: Find tests the regulated party applies to itself. Ask whether any registry, notice or record shows who decided it is covered or not, and who can check.

patterns.name: No anti-evasion clause
patterns.plain: The bill contains no provision that reaches conduct restructured, relabeled or routed through another person to fall outside the mandate.
patterns.fix: Add an anti-avoidance clause covering arrangements whose main purpose is to avoid the rule.
patterns.check: Look for any rule reaching conduct that is restructured, relabeled or routed through another person. Ask what stops a party from arranging around the mandate.

patterns.name: No substance-over-form backstop
patterns.plain: Compliance is judged by form alone, so arrangements with no purpose beyond avoiding the rule still qualify.
patterns.fix: Add a rule that arrangements without a purpose other than avoidance are disregarded.
patterns.check: Find compliance tests judged by form alone. Ask whether an arrangement with no purpose beyond avoiding the rule could still qualify.

patterns.name: Thresholds without aggregation
patterns.plain: A size, volume or notification threshold applies entity by entity or transaction by transaction, so splitting activity into parts avoids it.
patterns.fix: Add aggregation rules treating related entities and linked transactions as one.
patterns.ex_ai: A minimum size below which a deployment is ignored can exempt many small deployments that together have large effects.
patterns.check: Find size, volume or notice thresholds that apply entity by entity or transaction by transaction. Ask whether splitting activity would avoid them.

patterns.name: Blending to qualify
patterns.plain: Favored activity or property can be added so that a mixed whole meets a test.
patterns.fix: Measure the test on the underlying components and add a rule against adding items mainly to meet it.
patterns.check: Find tests applied to a mixed whole, such as a share or ratio. Ask whether favored items could be added to meet the test, and how the mix is measured and checked.

patterns.name: Uncovered close substitute
patterns.plain: A rule names one item, asset type or instrument and a near-equivalent is left outside it.
patterns.fix: Define the covered category by function and include close substitutes, with a power to extend it by rule.
patterns.check: Find rules naming one item, asset or instrument. Ask what close equivalent is left outside, and whether the purpose would be served by covering it.

patterns.name: Recharacterization into a favored category
patterns.plain: Income, activity or a worker's status can be relabeled to enter a category with lighter treatment.
patterns.fix: Add a substance based test for the favored category and a rule that disregards relabeling without a change in substance.
patterns.check: Find categories with lighter treatment. Ask whether income, activity or status could be relabeled to enter them, and who checks the label.

patterns.name: Unequal treatment of close equivalents
patterns.plain: Two near-identical activities are treated very differently, so parties gain by shifting between them.
patterns.fix: Align the treatment of close equivalents, or add a rule limiting the benefit of shifting.
patterns.check: Compare treatment of near identical activities. Ask whether the difference is large enough that parties would shift between them, and whether the purpose justifies it.

patterns.name: Round-trip transactions
patterns.plain: A transaction can be sent to another party or place and then returned to collect a benefit.
patterns.fix: Add a rule denying the benefit to transactions that return to the original party or place, and require reporting.
patterns.check: Look for benefits tied to a location, party or category. Ask whether a transaction could be sent out and returned to collect the benefit.

patterns.name: Related-party attribution gap
patterns.plain: Family members, trusts or affiliates are not attributed to the covered person, so limits can be multiplied or avoided.
patterns.fix: Add attribution rules that treat related persons and controlled entities as one for each limit.
patterns.check: Find limits that apply to one person. Ask whether family members, trusts or affiliates are attributed to that person, and whether limits could be multiplied.

patterns.name: Duty on one link in a chain
patterns.plain: An obligation binds one actor while affiliates, intermediaries or controlling persons remain free to do the same thing.
patterns.fix: Extend the duty to controlling persons and intermediaries, or add a rule making them answerable for evasion.
patterns.check: Identify the one actor the duty binds. Ask whether affiliates, intermediaries or controlling persons could do the same thing outside the duty.

patterns.name: Election into a lighter parallel regime
patterns.plain: A party can choose to register or qualify under a second law that places lighter duties on it.
patterns.fix: State which set of rules governs when more than one applies, and bar a party from choosing the lighter set for the same activity.
patterns.check: Find other laws under which a party could register or qualify with lighter duties. Ask whether this bill addresses that choice.

patterns.name: Timing moves around a date
patterns.plain: Parties can move transactions across an effective date or holding period.
patterns.fix: Add a look back period (a span of earlier time that is examined) and a rule disregarding transactions timed mainly to fall on the favorable side of a date.
patterns.check: Find effective dates and holding periods. Ask whether transactions could be moved across them, and whether a look back rule (which examines earlier transactions) or a rule against timing transactions exists.

patterns.name: Netting that cancels a charge
patterns.plain: Offset rules, which subtract credits, can reduce a new tax or duty toward zero.
patterns.fix: Cap the offsets, or set a minimum amount that netting cannot reduce.
patterns.check: Find offset, credit and netting rules (rules that subtract one amount from another) attached to a new charge or duty. Ask whether they could reduce it toward zero.

patterns.name: Offsetting response by another government
patterns.plain: A state or other government can redesign its own law to cancel out the effect of the federal limit.
patterns.fix: Add a rule that addresses offsetting changes by other governments, and a duty to report on those changes so they can be tracked.
patterns.check: Find limits placed on another level of government. Ask whether that government could redesign its own law to cancel out the limit, and whether the bill's text anticipates that.

patterns.name: Single enforcer
patterns.plain: Only one federal agency may enforce the law, and state attorneys general have no parallel authority to enforce it.
patterns.fix: Give state officials parallel enforcement authority, and allow a private right of action as an additional way to enforce.
patterns.check: Find who may enforce the bill. Ask whether state officials or others have parallel authority, and what happens if the one enforcer does not act.

patterns.name: No reward for insiders
patterns.plain: The bill at most protects whistleblowers and offers no relator suit (a suit by a private person for the government) or bounty (a share of money recovered).
patterns.fix: Add a right for insiders to report violations with a share of the money recovered, and add protection from retaliation.
patterns.check: Look for protection, rewards or the right to sue for insiders who report violations. Ask whether reporting carries any benefit beyond protection from retaliation.

patterns.name: Private right without economics
patterns.plain: A right to sue exists, but the bill gives no fixed or multiplied damages and no way to recover legal fees, so small claims are not worth bringing.
patterns.fix: Add fixed or multiplied damages, and let a plaintiff who wins recover reasonable legal fees.
patterns.check: Find any right to sue and read the remedies. Ask whether damages, multiples of damages or shifting of legal fees to the losing side make a small claim worth bringing.

patterns.name: Fees lost on voluntary compliance
patterns.plain: Fee shifting applies only to judgments, so a defendant can comply after being sued and avoid paying fees.
patterns.fix: Allow fees where the lawsuit led to the change in conduct, not only after a judgment.
patterns.check: Read the fee shifting terms. Ask whether fees are available only after a judgment, and whether a defendant could comply after being sued and avoid them.

patterns.name: Non-enforcement left unreviewable
patterns.plain: No standards or triggers say when the agency must enforce. As a result, a decision not to enforce, including a decision covering a whole category of cases, cannot be challenged.
patterns.fix: State criteria or triggers for enforcement, allow review of a refusal to enforce, and add a duty to report.
patterns.check: Find the standards for when the agency must enforce. Ask whether a decision not to enforce, including one covering a whole category of cases, can be challenged.

patterns.name: Statutory damages without concrete harm
patterns.plain: Fixed damages for a bare violation, meaning one with no proven harm, leave many plaintiffs without standing (the right to sue) in federal court.
patterns.fix: Define the injury that the fixed damages provision addresses, allow other enforcers to sue, and provide an alternative forum.
patterns.check: Find fixed damages for a bare violation, meaning a violation with no proven harm. Ask whether a plaintiff must show concrete harm to sue in federal court, and which plaintiffs would be left out.

patterns.name: Agency penalties without a court path
patterns.plain: Civil penalties can be imposed only in the agency's own tribunal, and that arrangement is open to a challenge claiming a right to a jury trial.
patterns.fix: Provide a court action for penalties as an alternative to the agency's tribunal.
patterns.check: Find civil penalties imposed in the agency's own tribunal. Ask whether a route through the courts exists, and whether a challenge claiming a right to a jury trial could stall them.

patterns.name: Funding conditions without rights language
