patterns.plain: Duties are written as conditions on grants without clear terms creating rights, so the people the grants are meant to help cannot sue.
patterns.fix: Use express language that creates rights, and state who may enforce it.
patterns.check: Find duties written as conditions on grants. Ask whether the text uses clear language creating rights, and whether the people who benefit could sue.

patterns.name: Independence resting on removal protection
patterns.plain: The design assumes that the officials who enforce the law cannot be removed at will.
patterns.fix: Add a substitute structure that keeps the body's function if removal protection is invalidated.
patterns.check: Find protections that assume enforcers cannot be removed at will. Ask what happens to the design if a court finds those protections invalid.

patterns.name: Missing clear statement on states
patterns.plain: The bill changes the balance of power between the federal government and the states, or subjects states to lawsuits, without the explicit statement that courts require.
patterns.fix: State the intended effect on state governments in clear, express terms.
patterns.check: Find provisions that change the balance between the federal government and the states or that subject states to suit. Ask whether the text says so explicitly, in the way courts require.

patterns.name: Mental state unstated or set high
patterns.plain: A penalty provision says nothing about the violator's mental state, or liability attaches only to "willful" or "knowing" violations.
patterns.fix: State the required mental state, and provide for civil liability without proof of intent.
patterns.check: Find penalty provisions and read the mental state they require, meaning what the violator must have known or intended. Ask whether it is unstated, or limited to 'willful' or 'knowing' acts, and what a regulated party could claim not to know.

patterns.name: Ambiguity in a penalty provision
patterns.plain: Unclear words in a provision carrying criminal penalties are read in the defendant's favor, and that reading can also be applied in civil cases.
patterns.fix: Define the key terms of any penalty provision, and separate the civil standard from the criminal standard.
patterns.check: Find unclear words in provisions carrying criminal penalties. Ask whether the narrower reading would be applied, and whether that reading could also be applied in civil cases.

patterns.name: Narrowing by constitutional doubt
patterns.plain: A party can win a narrow reading of a law by raising a serious constitutional question, even without winning the constitutional claim itself.
patterns.fix: Include a clear statement of how broadly the provision is meant to apply, and findings that support the provision.
patterns.check: Find provisions that could raise a serious constitutional question. Ask whether a court could adopt a narrow reading to avoid it.

patterns.name: Gates on private suits
patterns.plain: A mandatory notice period, a bar while the government is "diligently prosecuting" (actively pursuing its own case), or a government power to dismiss can stop a private suit.
patterns.fix: Limit the notice period, define when a government action blocks a private suit, and require court approval of dismissals.
patterns.check: Find notice periods, bars on suits while the government is prosecuting, and government powers to dismiss. Ask whether any of them could stop a private suit before it proceeds.

patterns.name: Private relator open to challenge
patterns.plain: Enforcement by relators, who sue on the government's behalf, faces unresolved objections under Article II of the Constitution.
patterns.fix: Add a government enforcement path that continues if the system of suits by private relators is invalidated.
patterns.check: Find enforcement by private parties on the government's behalf. Ask what constitutional objections could be raised and what happens if they succeed.

patterns.name: Past violations not actionable
patterns.plain: Private suits reach only ongoing or future violations, or only relief that looks forward.
patterns.fix: Allow suits over past violations within a stated period, and provide for damages as well as relief that applies to the future.
patterns.check: Read what private suits may reach. Ask whether past violations can be sued over or only ongoing ones, and whether only relief that applies to the future is available.

patterns.name: Limitation period that never restarts
patterns.plain: The limitation period, which is the time allowed to sue, runs from the first act and does not restart with each continuing effect.
patterns.fix: State that each continuing violation or new effect starts a new limitation period.
patterns.check: Find limitation periods, meaning deadlines to sue, and when each one starts. Ask whether each continuing effect restarts the deadline or only the first act counts.

patterns.name: No time limit on rule challenges
patterns.plain: The bill relies on the general six-year time limit, which restarts for each newly injured party.
patterns.fix: State a specific filing period for challenges, and state when it starts.
patterns.check: Look for a time limit on challenges to rules made under the bill. Ask whether the general default time limit applies and when it restarts.

patterns.name: Filing rule readable as jurisdictional
patterns.plain: A deadline or precondition is worded so that a court treats it as a limit on its own power, not as a rule that can be waived.
patterns.fix: Word deadlines as claim processing rules, which are ordinary procedural rules, and state that they may be waived or tolled (paused).
patterns.check: Find deadlines and preconditions to suit. Ask whether the wording could be read as a limit on the court's power instead of a rule that can be waived.

patterns.name: Private trigger open to misuse
patterns.plain: A private notice or complaint can force action, but the bill sets no penalty for false notices, no counter-notice and too little time to verify.
patterns.fix: Add a penalty for false notices, a counter notice process and a reasonable period for verification.
patterns.check: Find private notices or complaints that compel action. Ask what penalizes false ones, whether a counter notice process exists, and whether the time allowed to verify them is enough.

patterns.name: Enforcement gated by vote or profit
patterns.plain: A penalty requires a political vote before it applies, or recovery is limited to profit that the violator actually realized.
patterns.fix: Remove the vote requirement, and allow recovery beyond profit, such as damages or fixed penalties.
patterns.check: Find penalties that need a vote before they apply, and recovery limited to realized profit. Ask who controls the vote and whether the cap makes a violation inexpensive for the violator.

patterns.name: Dollar figures not indexed
patterns.plain: Penalties, caps and thresholds are fixed dollar amounts that lose value or drift as inflation changes prices.
patterns.fix: Index dollar figures to a named measure with a scheduled adjustment.
patterns.check: List each fixed dollar penalty, cap and threshold. Ask whether it is indexed (adjusted automatically for inflation), and what it will be worth after several years of inflation.

patterns.name: Penalties deductible or untracked
patterns.plain: Nothing in the bill bars penalties from being deducted, and nothing says where penalty money goes.
patterns.fix: Bar the deduction of penalties, and direct where penalty receipts are deposited and reported.
patterns.check: Find how the bill treats penalty payments. Ask whether they can be deducted or recovered from others, and where the money goes.

patterns.name: Appropriated funds can be withheld
patterns.plain: Money is appropriated, but nothing forces it to be committed for spending on time, and nothing lets anyone sue if it is held back.
patterns.fix: Add a deadline for committing the funds, and a duty to report on delays.
patterns.check: Find appropriations (money set aside by law for spending) and ask whether anything forces the money to be committed on time. Ask whether anyone can sue if the money is held back.

patterns.name: Funding that depends on a request
patterns.plain: Mandatory funding is paid only when the agency head asks for it or a contested formula term is met.
patterns.fix: Provide funding by default, with the request or formula acting as an adjustment rather than a condition.
patterns.check: Find funding that is paid only on a request or when a formula term is met. Ask who controls the request, and what happens if no one makes it.

patterns.name: Offsets that score without changing outlays
patterns.plain: Changes to mandatory programs, or repeated delay of a rule that was never in force, are counted as savings.
patterns.fix: Report the savings and the basis for counting them, and require a review of actual outlays.
patterns.src: Taxpayers for Common Sense; NTU Foundation
patterns.check: Find savings used to pay for new spending. Ask whether they change actual outlays (money actually spent), or merely count the delay of a rule that was never in force.

patterns.name: Designations and timing shifts outside caps
patterns.plain: Emergency designations, advance appropriations and timing shifts take spending outside budget limits.
patterns.fix: Require a stated justification for each designation, and report the totals measured against the budget limits.
patterns.check: Find emergency designations, advance appropriations and timing shifts. Ask whether they move spending outside budget limits.

patterns.name: Spending authority outside appropriations
patterns.plain: Contract or borrowing authority lets funds be committed without an appropriation.
patterns.fix: Require an appropriation, or a reporting and review step, before any commitment is made.
patterns.check: Find contract or borrowing authority. Ask whether it commits funds without an appropriation, and who reviews the commitments.

patterns.name: Provision shaped to a reconciliation test
patterns.plain: A provision is sized, given an end date or worded to meet the Senate's Byrd rule on budget reconciliation bills.
patterns.fix: Disclose which provisions were shaped for the procedure, and review them after they become law.
patterns.check: Find provisions sized, dated or worded to meet a special budget procedure. Ask whether the provision's form departs from what the policy would otherwise need.

patterns.name: Serial short-term renewal
patterns.plain: Temporary provisions are renewed repeatedly instead of being made permanent or ended.
patterns.fix: Set a longer term, or a review that leads to a decision to make the provision permanent or to end it.
patterns.check: Find temporary provisions and their expiry dates. Ask whether they have been renewed before, and whether making them permanent or ending them is an option.

patterns.name: Mandate silent on who pays
patterns.plain: A requirement is imposed without saying which party bears its cost.
patterns.fix: State who bears the cost and how, with funding or cost sharing where needed.
patterns.check: Find each requirement and ask which party bears its cost. Check whether the text says so, and ask what happens if that party cannot pay.

patterns.name: Overlapping benefits with no offset
patterns.plain: Two programs pay for the same period or need with no coordination clause.
patterns.fix: Add a coordination clause that provides for an offset or a priority between the programs.
patterns.check: Find programs that pay for the same period or need. Ask whether a clause coordinates them, and whether double payment is possible.

patterns.name: Amendatory instruction that cannot be executed
patterns.plain: An instruction to strike, insert or renumber words in an existing law is ambiguous or does not match the text it amends.
patterns.fix: Verify each instruction against the current text of the amended law before the bill becomes law.
patterns.check: Check each instruction to strike, insert or renumber text against the text it amends. Ask whether it can be carried out exactly as written.

patterns.name: Amendatory reference to the wrong law
patterns.plain: Inside quoted inserted text, "this Act" or "the date of enactment of this Act" refers to the amended law, not the new bill.
patterns.fix: Name the intended law and date expressly inside the inserted text.
patterns.check: Read quoted inserted text for the phrases 'this Act' and 'date of enactment of this Act'. Ask whether each points to the amended law or to the new bill.

patterns.name: Citation to the wrong source of law
patterns.plain: A bill amends the Code for a title that is not positive law, or amends the Act for a title that is positive law.
patterns.fix: Use the correct citation form for each title and confirm it with the codifiers.
patterns.check: Check whether each amendment targets the Code or the Act, and whether the title is positive law. Ask whether the citation form fits the title.

patterns.name: Broken, circular or chained cross-reference
patterns.plain: A reference points to the wrong part of the law, to itself, or to a series of other references.
patterns.fix: Replace chained references with direct ones and check that each target exists.
patterns.check: Follow each cross-reference to its target. Ask whether it points to the right part of the law, to itself, or through a chain of other references.

patterns.name: Repeal or sunset with unintended survivors
patterns.plain: A repeal does not bring back the prior law, and a sunset (an end date for an authority) leaves the amendments the Act made in force.
patterns.fix: State which provisions and amendments end, and whether earlier law is restored.
patterns.check: Read each repeal and sunset. Ask whether prior law returns, and whether amendments made by the Act stay in force after the authority ends.

patterns.name: Repeal silent on accrued liabilities
patterns.plain: A repeal or expiry does not say whether penalties already incurred survive, so the general savings statute decides the question.
patterns.fix: State whether accrued penalties and pending cases continue after repeal or expiry.
patterns.check: Read each repeal or expiry for how it treats penalties already incurred. Ask whether they survive or whether the general savings rule decides.

patterns.name: Effective date confused with applicability
patterns.plain: The bill does not distinguish the date the text takes effect from the persons, things or events it applies to.
patterns.fix: State the effective date and the rule on who or what the bill applies to in separate provisions.
patterns.check: Find each effective date. Ask whether the text separates the date it takes effect from the persons, things and events it applies to.

patterns.name: No transitional rules
patterns.plain: The bill changes current programs or behavior without saying how existing cases move to the new rule.
patterns.fix: Add transitional provisions covering pending matters and a schedule for existing cases.
patterns.check: Look for rules on how existing cases, contracts and programs move to the new rule. Ask what happens to those in progress on the effective date.

patterns.name: Substantive rule stranded in an amending act
patterns.plain: A free-standing rule sits in an amending or temporary section, where it will not be codified (placed in the official Code) with the parent law.
patterns.fix: Place the rule in the parent law or state how it is to be codified.
patterns.check: Find free standing rules in amending or temporary sections. Ask whether they will be codified with the parent law and whether readers will find them.

patterns.name: Restatement of other law
patterns.plain: A provision repeats existing law, which creates two sources of the same rule that can diverge.
patterns.fix: Cross-refer to the existing law instead of restating it, or state which text governs.
patterns.check: Find provisions repeating existing law. Ask whether the two sources could diverge, and which one governs if they do.

patterns.name: Conflict with international obligations
patterns.plain: The measure conflicts with a treaty or trade commitment, and general language saying the measure overrides other law does not reach that conflict.
patterns.fix: Add an express statement on the relationship to those obligations and a review step.
patterns.src: Senate manual sec. 314(b)(2)(B); Kamin et al.
patterns.check: Compare the measure with treaty and trade commitments. Ask whether any conflict exists, and whether general language overriding other law reaches it.

patterns.name: Boilerplate relied on beyond its function
patterns.plain: Stock phrases such as a general override or a routine severability clause, which keeps the rest of a law in force if part is struck down, are treated as protective.
patterns.fix: Replace boilerplate with specific text where protection matters, such as named provisions or tailored severability.
patterns.check: Find standard clauses such as a general override or a severability clause. Ask whether they actually protect what the drafters think they protect.

patterns.name: No protection from later implied override
patterns.plain: Nothing requires a later law to refer expressly to this bill before replacing it.
patterns.fix: Add a clause requiring any later law that would displace this bill to refer to it expressly.
patterns.check: Look for any rule that requires a later law to refer expressly to this bill before replacing it. Ask whether a later law could override this bill silently.

patterns.name: No fallback if struck down
patterns.plain: No substitute rule takes effect if a court invalidates the primary provision.
patterns.fix: Add a fallback rule that takes effect if the primary provision is invalidated.
patterns.check: Find the primary provision and ask what applies if a court invalidates it. Ask whether any substitute takes effect.

patterns.name: Linked provisions not tied together
patterns.plain: Provisions enacted as a package are not made inseverable, meaning tied so that they stand or fall together, so a court can remove one of the linked provisions.
patterns.fix: State which provisions stand or fall together and add a fallback.
patterns.check: Find provisions enacted as a package or bargain. Ask whether the text makes them inseverable, and what remains if a court removes one of them.

patterns.name: No fast track for validity challenges
patterns.plain: Constitutional challenges follow ordinary procedure, so the law's status stays uncertain for years.
patterns.fix: Provide expedited review, a single forum and direct appeal for validity challenges.
patterns.check: Look for expedited procedure for constitutional challenges. Ask how long the law's status could stay uncertain under ordinary procedure.

patterns.name: Savings clause not stopping implied preemption
patterns.plain: A clause preserving state law does not prevent a finding of conflict preemption (federal law displacing state law that conflicts with it), and loose terms such as "requirements" can reach common-law claims.
patterns.fix: Add an express statement that conflict preemption does not apply to preserved state law, and define 'requirements'.
patterns.check: Read each clause preserving state law. Ask whether it stops a finding of conflict preemption, and whether words such as 'requirements' reach common law claims, which are claims based on court-made law.

patterns.name: Preemption without a replacement standard
patterns.plain: State rules are displaced, but the federal government sets no replacement standard, so no regulation applies.
patterns.fix: Pair displacement with a federal standard, or limit displacement to areas that the federal rule covers.
patterns.check: Find provisions displacing state rules. Ask what federal standard replaces them, and what level of regulation remains.

patterns.name: Funding conditions that deter state rules
patterns.plain: Grant eligibility is used to discourage state or local regulation.
patterns.fix: Limit conditions to how the funds are used, and state that eligibility does not depend on giving up state rules.
patterns.check: Find grant eligibility terms that concern state or local regulation. Ask whether they discourage governments from adopting their own rules.

patterns.name: No anti-backsliding rule
patterns.plain: Standards, permits or plans can be revised downward at renewal, and no minimum level prevents it.
patterns.fix: Add a rule that a revision may not be less protective than the existing standard unless a finding is stated.
patterns.check: Find provisions for revising standards, permits or plans. Ask whether any minimum level prevents a downward revision at renewal.

patterns.name: No construction rule for coverage
patterns.plain: No instruction says that coverage terms are to be read broadly to serve the bill's purpose.
patterns.fix: Add a rule that coverage terms are to be read in the way that serves the bill's purpose, and state exceptions narrowly.
patterns.check: Look for an instruction on how broadly coverage terms are to be read. Ask whether a narrow reading would defeat the bill's stated purpose.

patterns.name: Later ratification of a lenient reading
patterns.plain: Reenactment without change lets a party argue that Congress accepted a narrow reading by an agency or court.
patterns.fix: State in the text that reenactment does not approve any prior reading.
patterns.check: Find provisions reenacted without change after an agency or court read them narrowly. Ask whether a party could argue that the legislature accepted that reading.

patterns.name: Orphaned functions after a sunset
patterns.plain: The administering body expires while its contracts, licenses or fee collections continue, and no successor is named.
patterns.fix: Name a successor body and provide for the transfer of functions when an agency ends under a sunset.
patterns.check: Find bodies that expire, and ask what happens to their contracts, licenses and fee collections. Ask whether a successor is named.

patterns.name: No authority to correct a known flaw
patterns.plain: The agency cannot fix an acknowledged error or distortion without new legislation.
patterns.fix: Add a limited correction authority with notice, a stated finding and a reporting duty.
patterns.check: Look for authority to fix an acknowledged error without new legislation. Ask what the agency could do if a flaw appears.

patterns.name: Eligibility by self-attestation
patterns.plain: A benefit or status is established by the applicant's own statement, and verification is barred or not required.
patterns.fix: Allow verification and audit of attestations (applicants' own statements) after the fact, with penalties for false statements.
patterns.check: Find benefits or status established by the applicant's own statement. Ask whether verification is allowed, barred or required.

patterns.name: Bar on sharing data between agencies
patterns.plain: A law's wording or silence stops one agency from giving another agency the data it needs.
patterns.fix: Add an express data sharing authority, with safeguards.
patterns.check: Read confidentiality and privacy language. Ask whether it stops one agency from giving another the data it needs to carry out the bill.

patterns.name: Decision rule decoupled from its drivers
patterns.plain: A decision is separated in time from the choices that make it necessary, and inaction produces an outcome that no one intends.
patterns.fix: Set a default outcome that matches the intended policy and require a decision before the default applies.
patterns.check: Find decisions set apart in time from the choices that make them necessary. Ask what happens if no one acts, and whether that result is intended.

patterns.name: No backstop for delegated implementers
patterns.plain: States or other delegates carry out the program, and nothing provides for the federal government to act in their place if they do not.
patterns.fix: Provide a federal default or takeover if the delegate does not carry out the program.
patterns.check: Find programs carried out by states or other delegates. Ask what happens if a delegate does not act, and whether a default exists, meaning a rule under which the federal government acts instead.

patterns.name: No scheduled review of standards
patterns.plain: Standards are set once and coverage shrinks as conditions change.
patterns.fix: Add a scheduled review with a duty to update and report.
patterns.check: Look for a review date for standards set in the bill. Ask whether coverage could shrink as conditions change.

patterns.name: Review duty with a built-in exit
patterns.plain: A periodic review or report can be skipped on the agency's own decision.
patterns.fix: Make the review mandatory and require a published reason for any extension.
patterns.check: Find periodic reviews and reports. Ask whether the agency may skip them on its own decision.

patterns.name: Power to exempt whole classes
patterns.plain: An agency may exempt "any entity or class of entities" on a broad public-interest finding.
patterns.fix: Limit the exemption power by named criteria, time limits and public notice.
patterns.check: Find powers to exempt 'any entity or class of entities'. Ask what criteria limit the power, and what limits the number or size of the groups exempted.

patterns.name: Unrecorded waivers and exemptions
patterns.plain: Waivers are granted with no public record of how many or to whom.
patterns.fix: Require a public register (a published list) of each waiver, and an annual report.
patterns.check: Look for a public record of waivers and exemptions. Ask whether anyone can learn how many were granted and to whom.

patterns.name: Narrowing or deferral after enactment
patterns.plain: Regulations issued under a general grant of power narrow what the statute covers, or a later amendment postpones duties before they apply.
patterns.fix: Set the core terms in the statute and add a reporting duty on any narrowing or deferral.
patterns.check: Find general grants of rulemaking power and the risk of later amendment. Ask whether regulations could narrow the statute, or a later law could postpone duties before they apply.

patterns.name: Agency barred from supplying a definition
patterns.plain: Congress blocks the agency from issuing the rule that would supply the definition the text lacks.
patterns.fix: State the definition in the bill, or allow a narrow rule to supply it.
patterns.check: Find limits on the agency's power to issue rules. Ask what is left undefined as a result, and who supplies the missing definition.

patterns.name: Advisory-only or removable watchdog
patterns.plain: A review body can only recommend, or an inspector can be removed without notice and reasons.
patterns.fix: Give the body binding duties to follow up, and require notice and reasons for removal.
patterns.check: Find review bodies and inspectors. Ask whether they can only recommend, and whether removal needs notice and reasons.

patterns.name: Structural checks that can stall the agency
patterns.plain: Quorum rules (the minimum number of members needed to act) or supermajority rules let unfilled seats halt the agency's work.
patterns.fix: Add a substitute rule for when there is no quorum, and a deadline for filling seats.
patterns.check: Find quorum and supermajority rules. Ask whether unfilled seats could halt the agency, and what substitute rule applies.

patterns.name: Deadline that distorts priorities
patterns.plain: A rigid deadline or automatic default forces action on one duty at the cost of rushed rules or neglect of others.
patterns.fix: Set priorities among duties and allow a stated extension with reasons.
patterns.check: Find rigid deadlines and automatic defaults. Ask whether they could force action on one duty at the cost of rushed rules or neglect of others.

patterns.name: Many independent clearance points
patterns.plain: Many separate sign-offs are required before action can be taken.
patterns.fix: Reduce the number of approvals, set a time limit for each and add a default if one is missed.
patterns.check: Count the separate sign offs required before action can be taken. Ask whether any one of them can block action, and whether a time limit applies to each.

patterns.name: Administrative burden on beneficiaries
patterns.plain: Paperwork and other burdens keep eligible people from a right or benefit that exists in the law's text but is hard to claim.
patterns.fix: Simplify the process, allow automatic enrollment where possible, and require reporting on how many eligible people take up the benefit.
patterns.check: Trace the steps a person must take to claim a right or benefit. Ask how much paperwork and delay is involved, and who bears the cost.

patterns.name: No built-in evaluation or data plan
patterns.plain: No clause requires a review against the bill's purpose or secures the data needed to do it, and any review is done by the implementing body.
patterns.fix: Add an independent evaluation duty with a data plan and a published report.
patterns.check: Look for a clause requiring review against the stated purpose and securing the data needed to do it. Ask who performs the review.

patterns.name: Powers never commenced or used
patterns.plain: Authority is granted but never brought into operation, and no duty requires a report on why.
patterns.fix: Add a commencement date and a duty to report why any power has not been used.
patterns.check: Find powers that need a start date or a first act. Ask whether any duty requires them to be brought into operation or reported on if not used.

patterns.name: Reform that codifies existing practice
patterns.plain: A new rule would have changed almost no past cases.
patterns.fix: Add a measurable change or a review of whether the rule alters practice.
patterns.check: Compare the new rule with current practice. Ask how many past cases it would have changed.

patterns.name: Committee review bypassed
patterns.plain: Text passes under emergency or leadership procedure, or a draft is enacted without the expected stage for correcting technical errors.
patterns.fix: Require committee review and a posting period before the full chamber acts, and a technical review of the final text.
patterns.check: Check how the text moved through the process. Ask whether it passed under emergency or leadership procedure, and whether the stage for correcting technical errors was skipped.

patterns.name: Externally drafted or model text
patterns.plain: Bill text is drafted by an outside organization or copied closely from one.
patterns.fix: Require disclosure of outside drafters and a review of the text against the bill's purpose.
patterns.check: Compare the text with outside documents. Ask whether it was drafted by or copied from an outside organization, and whether that is disclosed.

patterns.name: Automatic effect absent disapproval
patterns.plain: A board's or official's recommendation takes effect unless Congress acts to stop it.
patterns.fix: Require an affirmative approval step, or a clear time window and procedure for disapproval.
patterns.check: Find recommendations that take effect unless the legislature acts. Ask who can stop them, how quickly, and what happens if no one does.

patterns.name: Expedited procedure that limits amendment
patterns.plain: Expedited procedures restrict debate and amendment.
patterns.fix: Allow amendment and a minimum period of debate, or limit expedited procedure to defined cases.
patterns.check: Find expedited procedures. Ask what debate and amendment they allow, and what changes could not be made.

patterns.name: Authority to skip public comment
patterns.plain: Rules can take effect before or without public comment through good-cause exceptions, interim final rules or guidance documents.
patterns.fix: Limit skipping comment to stated circumstances, set an end date on interim rules, and require notice and comment later.
patterns.check: Find routes that allow rules to take effect without comment, such as good cause or interim final rules. Ask what limits them.

patterns.name: No comparative print
patterns.plain: The bill is drafted so that no document shows how it changes existing law.
patterns.fix: Require a comparative print to be published before consideration.
patterns.src: House Rules and Manual; Senate rules
patterns.check: Look for a document showing how the bill changes existing law. Ask whether readers can see the changes without assembling them.

patterns.name: No cost or regulatory impact statement
patterns.plain: The report that accompanies the bill lacks a cost estimate or regulatory impact evaluation.
patterns.fix: Require a cost estimate and impact evaluation before consideration.
patterns.check: Look for a cost estimate and a regulatory impact evaluation with the bill. Ask who prepared them and whether they cover the main provisions.

patterns.name: No agency technical review
patterns.plain: The bill was drafted without technical assistance from the agency that will administer it.
patterns.fix: Request and publish a technical review from the administering agency before enactment.
patterns.check: Look for technical assistance from the agency that will administer the bill. Ask whether the text was reviewed for workability.

patterns.name: Provision added or dropped late
patterns.plain: A safeguard, a corrective provision or a protective provision is added to or removed from a must-pass bill late in the process.
patterns.fix: Require a posting period for late changes and a record of what was added or dropped.
patterns.check: Compare earlier versions of the bill with the final text. Ask what was added or removed late, especially safeguards, corrective provisions and protective provisions.

patterns.name: Drafting and reading conventions differ
patterns.plain: Drafters do not follow several canons (rules of interpretation) that courts apply, so text is read in ways its authors did not expect.
patterns.fix: Have the text reviewed against common interpretive canons and add construction rules where they differ.
patterns.check: Compare the drafting style with the canons courts apply. Ask where the text could be read in ways its authors did not expect.

patterns.name: Procedure that favors a constituency
patterns.plain: Procedural rules give particular groups special access to information, the right to sue, or chances to block action.
patterns.fix: Open procedural rights to all affected parties, and require public notice of key steps.
patterns.src: McCubbins, Noll and Weingast, from a scholar's notes
patterns.check: Read procedural rules for who receives information, the right to sue, or chances to block action. Ask whether a particular group gains an advantage.

patterns.name: Cross-reference that rots after enactment
patterns.plain: A law can borrow a definition or a list by citing a numbered part of another law. The borrowing is right on the day it is enacted. A later law can then renumber the cited part, so the citation points at different words, or at nothing. Neither law has to change what it says, and no one amends the borrowing law, so its own text gives no sign that its reach has moved.
patterns.fix: Set the borrowed words out in the text itself where the list is short and settled. Where a citation is used, name the subject of the cited part as well as its number, so a reader can still find the content after a renumbering. Freeze the reference to the law as in effect on the date of enactment only where a fixed meaning is intended, because freezing it also stops later corrections from reaching it.
patterns.src: Protecting Americans' Data from Foreign Adversaries Act of 2024, Public Law 118-50
patterns.check: List every place the text borrows a definition, a list or a standard by citing a numbered part of another law. Open each cited part today and confirm it still holds what the borrowing text assumes. Then ask what the borrowing text would mean if that part were renumbered, and whether anything in the text would show it had happened.

patterns.name: The party judges its own compliance
patterns.plain: The same person or body carries out a duty and also decides whether the duty was met. Examples are a party that certifies its own work, declares its own task complete or writes the only report on its own conduct.
patterns.fix: Look for an outside reviewer, an audit, or a deadline that does not depend on the party's own declaration.
patterns.check: Find every certification, completion date and report in the measure. Ask who produces each one and whether that party is also the one whose performance it describes.
patterns.ex_other: A House committee report in March 2020 found a failure of oversight by the Federal Aviation Administration in certifying the Boeing 737 MAX. Under a program that critics said created a conflict of interest, the agency had delegated some certification work to Boeing employees.

patterns.name: The party must investigate or disclose its own conduct
patterns.plain: A measure orders a body to investigate, release or report on matters that include that body's own past decisions, its leaders, or the people who appoint its leaders.
patterns.fix: Look for an independent decision-maker, a recusal rule, or outside review of what is withheld.
patterns.check: List what the measure tells the body to release or investigate. Ask whether any of it documents the body's own conduct or the conduct of people the body answers to.
patterns.ex_other: Congress created independent counsels in the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 because conflicts of interest can arise when the executive branch investigates its own officials. Congress let those provisions lapse in 1999.
patterns.src: Congressional Research Service, Special Counsel Investigations (R44857)

patterns.name: The holder depends on someone affected by the decision
patterns.plain: The official given the job is appointed by, reports to, or can be removed by a person whose interests the decision affects.
patterns.fix: Look for a fixed term, limits on removal, or a decision-maker outside that chain of command.
patterns.check: For each job in the measure, find who appoints and who can remove the holder. Ask whether that person is affected by the decisions the holder must make.
patterns.ex_other: The Inspector General Act lets the President remove most inspectors general after giving Congress 30 days' written notice of the reasons. The statute does not limit the grounds for removal, so their independence rests largely on deterrence and congressional oversight.
patterns.src: Congressional Research Service, Presidential Removal of IGs (LSB10476)

patterns.name: The current holder has a tie to an affected person
patterns.plain: The person who holds the job now has worked for, represented, funded or been funded by someone the measure affects. This type depends on who holds the office, so it can change when the officeholder changes.
patterns.fix: Look for a recusal rule and for a named substitute who decides when the holder steps aside.
patterns.check: Identify who currently holds each job. Research that person's past employers, clients and public roles, and compare them with the people and bodies the measure affects. Report a tie only with a source.

patterns.name: The decision-maker has money at stake
patterns.plain: The official who decides, or that official's family, would gain or lose money depending on the decision.
patterns.fix: Look for disclosure, divestment or recusal requirements written into the measure.
patterns.check: Ask whether the measure lets an official decide matters that affect companies or assets the official may own, and whether it relies on general ethics law or sets its own rule.
patterns.ex_other: A federal criminal statute, section 208 of title 18 of the United States Code, bars executive branch employees from taking part in matters that affect their own financial interests.

patterns.name: The deciding body is funded by its own decisions
patterns.plain: The body that decides keeps the fines, fees or property that result from its decisions, or is funded by the parties it oversees.
patterns.fix: Look for money that goes to a general fund, and for a budget that does not depend on the parties being overseen.
patterns.check: Trace where fines, fees and forfeited property go, and who pays for the body's budget. Ask whether the body's income rises when it decides one way.
patterns.ex_other: In Tumey v. Ohio (1927) the Supreme Court held that it violated due process for a judge to be paid from the fines imposed on the defendants he convicted. Separately, fees paid by drug companies now fund more than 65 percent of the Food and Drug Administration's human drugs program. Supporters cite faster reviews, and critics say the fees give industry undue influence.

patterns.name: One body must both promote and police the same activity
patterns.plain: A single agency is told to encourage an industry, or collect revenue from it, and also to enforce safety or other limits on it.
patterns.fix: Look for separate bodies, or separate leadership and budgets, for missions that pull in opposite directions.
patterns.check: List every mission the measure gives to one body. Ask whether success at one mission is made harder by strict performance of another.
patterns.ex_other: After the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, the Interior Department said the Minerals Management Service had inherently conflicted missions: resource management, safety oversight and revenue collection. The Department divided those missions among three separate offices in 2010 and 2011.

patterns.name: Regulated parties do the regulator's work
patterns.plain: The measure lets the parties being regulated write the standards, sit on the deciding body, or certify their own products or conduct.
patterns.fix: Look for a public agency that must approve the standard or the certification, and for limits on how many seats regulated parties hold.
patterns.check: Find every place the measure relies on industry standards, industry members of a board, or certification by the regulated party. Ask who checks that work.

patterns.name: The examiner is chosen or paid by the party it examines
patterns.plain: An auditor, rater, inspector or evaluator is selected or paid by the party whose work it must judge.
patterns.fix: Look for assignment of the examiner by a public body, for rotation, and for payment that does not come from the party examined.
patterns.check: For each audit, rating, inspection or evaluation in the measure, ask who selects the examiner and who pays.

patterns.name: The party that shapes the rules can then compete under them
patterns.plain: A contractor or grantee helps design a program, write its requirements or evaluate its results, and can then seek the contract or grant.
patterns.fix: Look for a rule that bars the advisor from competing, or that requires the conflict to be disclosed and reduced.
patterns.check: Ask whether the measure lets a party advise on requirements, standards or awards and also receive the resulting contracts or grants.
patterns.ex_other: Federal procurement rules call this an organizational conflict of interest. They cover a contractor that helps set the terms of a competition it can then enter, and a contractor whose other interests could impair its objectivity.
patterns.src: Congressional Research Service, Organizational Conflicts of Interest (LSB10772)

patterns.name: The body that writes the rule exempts itself
patterns.plain: The measure applies to others and leaves out the legislature, the executive office or the agency that wrote it.
patterns.fix: Look for wording that applies the rule to the body itself, or a separate office that applies it there.
patterns.check: Read the definitions and exceptions for any wording that leaves out Congress, the President, the courts or the agency in charge. Ask whether the reason given applies equally to those left in.
patterns.ex_other: Congress exempted itself from federal labor laws such as the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 when it passed them. The Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 applied many of those laws to Congress for the first time.

patterns.name: The overseen party controls the information the overseer needs
patterns.plain: The body being checked decides what information the checker receives, for example by classifying records, by self-reporting data or by deciding what counts as responsive.
patterns.fix: Look for a right of direct access to records, and for review of withholding by someone outside the body.
patterns.check: Ask what an overseer would need in order to test compliance, and who holds it. Ask whether the measure lets the overseen party withhold, summarize or classify that information.

patterns.name: The only enforcer has a reason not to enforce
patterns.plain: The measure can be enforced only by a body that is itself bound by the measure, or that is closely tied to the party that is bound.
patterns.fix: Look for a second enforcer, such as a right to sue, state attorneys general or an inspector general.
patterns.check: List everyone who can enforce the measure. Ask whether each one is independent of the party that owes the duty, and whether anyone else can act if that enforcer does not.

patterns.name: Decision-makers move between the regulator and the regulated
patterns.plain: The measure creates decisions of high value to an industry and sets no limit on officials who come from that industry or leave to work for it.
patterns.fix: Look for waiting periods, disclosure of job negotiations and limits on appointing recent industry employees.
patterns.check: Ask whether the measure creates new approvals, awards or enforcement choices, and whether it sets any waiting period before an official may work for an affected party.
